version.changelog: Initial release: AI-first credential management on Dash Platform

llm.summary: The skill's stated purpose (an AI-first credential vault) aligns with the included code, but there are multiple coherence problems — missing declared env/dependency requirements, a bundled CLI that reads/writes local secrets/cache, and unclear install expectations — so proceed with caution.

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md and the CLI implement a credential vault for Dash Platform and legitimately need access to a master key (WIF) and a Dash identity. However, the registry metadata declares no required environment variables or dependencies, which is inconsistent: the code and instructions require CRITICAL_WIF and DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID (and the @dashevo/evo-sdk package). This mismatch is unexpected and reduces transparency about what secrets and software are needed.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md limits scope to storing/retrieving/rotating credentials and documents a client-side encryption model. The bundled CLI performs exactly those actions. Concerns: (1) the code loads a .env.snapshot file from the skill directory via dotenv (it will also accept CRITICAL_WIF from process.env) — bundling or requiring a local .env file is surprising and can hide secrets; (2) the CLI decrypts credentials locally and returns plaintext to the caller (expected for a vault) — whether the agent can read or exfiltrate those plaintexts depends on the platform runtime; (3) the crypto code uses ECDH computeSecret with its own public key (computeSecret(ecdh.getPublicKey())), which is unusual for ECDH and may indicate a non-standard/buggy key derivation approach (the code does mitigate with per-credential salt/HKDF).
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec even though the repository includes runnable Node.js code that imports third-party modules (@dashevo/evo-sdk, dotenv). That means: (a) the skill will fail unless the runtime already has those Node modules; (b) the registry gives no info about what packages will be fetched/installed; (c) absence of an install step reduces reviewability and reproducibility. For a CLI that will be executed, a declared install or dependency list is expected.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requires high-sensitivity secrets at runtime: CRITICAL_WIF (master private key) and DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID (identity), but the registry declares no required env vars. The code also reads .env.snapshot (in the package dir) and derives a cache key from the WIF, writing an encrypted cache to ~/.dashpass/cache/credentials.enc. Requiring and using a private key is proportionate to a vault's purpose, but the lack of declared env requirements and the explicit expectation of a local .env.snapshot are red flags — the skill package may expect secrets to be placed in files bundled with the skill, which is dangerous and surprising.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always:true and does not modify other skills or global agent settings. It does persist an encrypted cache in the user's home (~/.dashpass/cache/) and will create directories there. Persisting an encrypted cache is reasonable for offline/fast access, but users should be aware the skill writes to the home directory and creates files with specific permissions.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Before installing or running this skill, consider the following: 1) Do not provide your mainnet private keys or any irreversible master credentials to untrusted code. Test with throwaway/testnet keys first. 2) The registry metadata does not declare env vars or Node dependencies — ask the publisher to declare required environment variables (CRITICAL_WIF, DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID) and a reproducible install (npm/yarn dependencies or an install script). 3) Inspect or request the .env.snapshot behavior: the CLI attempts to load .env.snapshot from the skill directory; verify no secret file is bundled in the skill and do not drop secrets into the skill directory. 4) Confirm how your agent runtime exposes environment variables and whether an autonomous agent could read CRITICAL_WIF or decrypted values — platform-level protections matter. 5) Review the included CLI code yourself or have someone you trust review it (note the unusual ECDH usage with computeSecret(ecdh.getPublicKey()) and ensure cryptographic design is acceptable). 6) Run the CLI in an isolated environment (VM or container) and with test credentials to validate behavior, and confirm the contract ID and identity are what you expect. 7) Ask the publisher for provenance (homepage / source repo / maintainer identity) and an install/dependency manifest before trusting the skill with real secrets.
